AMAX: A hedged mix held through other funds: long-term Treasury bonds, gold, stock funds and option-income strategies combined to pay income while blunting market drops. It's a defensive income holding, so it will lag in strong bull markets, and the protection comes from the blend rather than any single asset.
APOC: Exposure to America's largest companies with a defined shield over six-month periods starting each April and October: it is designed to protect against losses across the half year, in exchange for a cap on gains. The shorter cycle resets protection twice a year, so timing matters less than with annual versions.
AVNV: Value-priced companies outside the US, across developed large and small caps plus emerging markets, held through a family of sister funds. It leans toward cheaper stocks with stronger profits, so it works as the overseas value piece of a portfolio rather than a plain market holding.
DBEZ: Companies from the eurozone countries, led by banks, industrial firms and technology names, with the euro hedged back into dollars. The hedge is the point: it removes currency swings from the returns, so it does better than unhedged rivals when the euro weakens and worse when it strengthens.
DDFJ: Large US stocks in a two-way design over each year starting in January: it can gain when the market rises, up to a cap, and can also gain when the market dips a little, with a buffer against bigger drops. The trade-off is muted gains in a strong rally.
DDFY: Large US stocks arranged so the fund can gain in either direction over each year starting in May: it rises with the market up to a cap, and it can also gain when the market falls a little, with a buffer beyond that. The cost of the two-way design is smaller gains in a rally.
DDIV: Fifty large and mid-sized US stocks that combine the highest dividend yields with strong price momentum, led by banks and property trusts. It's an income fund with a momentum filter: the strength test is meant to weed out high yielders whose prices are collapsing.
DTEC: Companies across ten technology themes, from cybersecurity, cloud computing and robotics to clean energy, health innovation and mobile payments. It's a broad bet on disruptive technology in one fund, spread widely enough that no single theme or company dominates the result.
DVOL: Fifty large and mid-sized US stocks chosen for combining strong price momentum with the lowest swings, led by banks, industrials and property companies. It aims for a smoother core holding: the low-volatility filter should soften drops, though it can lag in sharp rallies led by riskier stocks.
EETH: Exposure to ether, the cryptocurrency of the Ethereum network, gained through futures contracts rather than holding the coin itself. It's a trading and hedging tool for crypto investors, and futures pricing means it can drift somewhat from ether's actual price over time.
FHDG: Large US stocks with a shock absorber that resets every quarter, where the size of the buffer is set dynamically rather than fixed in advance. It suits investors who want stock exposure with a softer landing, paid for with a cap on gains each quarter.
FPFD: Preferred shares and similar income securities, mostly from banks, pipelines and utilities, actively picked for their payouts. It plays the income role with steadier payments than common stocks, though preferred prices still fall when interest rates rise or bank credit worries grow.
FTOH: Ohio municipal bonds paying interest exempt from both federal and Ohio state income tax, with maturities of three years and longer. It's built for Ohio residents keeping more of their interest, and the single-state focus plus longer maturities mean more movement when rates change.
FTWO: Companies tied to natural resource and national security: farm machinery, defense, oil and gas, uranium and power utilities, mostly large US firms. It's a focused bet on the US securing its food, energy and defense supply lines, so it moves with those industries rather than the broad market.
GAA: A worldwide mix of stocks, bonds, real estate, commodities and currencies, held through other funds and tilted toward value and momentum. It's a set-and-forget allocation meant to grow steadily through different economies, and owning everything means it rarely leads in any single hot market.
GDXW: Gold mining companies, amplified: swap contracts target about a fifth more than the miners' own weekly move, with cash paid out every week. It's a leveraged trading tool on a volatile corner of the market, and the weekly reset makes it unsuitable as a long-term holding.
GLOW: Stocks from around the world, held through other funds covering US sectors and overseas markets, with at least two-fifths outside the US. It's a one-stop global holding run by a manager that shifts the mix between regions and sectors, so it can look quite different from a plain world index fund.
GTR: An options strategy on global stocks designed to land returns inside a target range, with most of the money parked in Treasury bills as collateral. It aims for modest, steadier gains rather than full market returns: big rallies are given up in exchange for a calmer range of outcomes.
GXPS: US consumer staples companies weighted purely by their market size, so the biggest food, drink, tobacco and household goods giants dominate. Staples are the defensive corner of the market; this pure version differs from rivals by applying no caps or tweaks, which makes it top-heavy in a few giants.
HQDG: Companies that pay dividends and have a record of raising them, spread fairly evenly across technology, industrials, health care and banks. It aims for income that grows over time as a core stock holding, and the even weighting keeps any single company from dominating.
HTEC: Companies using technology to change health care: genetic testing, diagnostics, surgical robotics, connected medical devices and health data software. It's a focused bet on medical innovation, heavy on smaller growth companies, so it can swing much more than a broad health care fund.
IBGA: US Treasury bonds all maturing in 2044, held in a fund that wraps up in December of that year. It's a bet on long-term government bonds: safe from default, but the long wait to maturity means its price swings a lot when interest rates change.
IBII: Inflation-protected US Treasury bonds all maturing in 2032, so the fund itself wraps up in October of that year. The principal grows with inflation, protecting purchasing power to a known end date, though the price still moves with interest rates along the way.
INKM: A global mix of stock, bond, real estate and preferred share funds, a bit under half in stocks, assembled purely to produce income. It's a conservative one-fund income portfolio: the blend steadies the payout, and returns will trail stock-heavy funds in strong markets.
JGRW: A concentrated handful of large US companies with long records of strong profitability, picked by active managers known for strict quality standards. Technology and health care lead; with few holdings, each pick matters, so it can trail the market for stretches when quality stocks fall out of favor.
JULV: Large US stocks paired with a buffer meant to absorb part of any loss over each year starting in July, in exchange for giving up some gains. It suits investors who want stock market exposure with a softer landing, and the protection in place depends on when you buy.
KARS: The electric vehicle world in one fund: car makers, battery producers, chip suppliers and charging and materials companies from the US, China, Europe and Japan. It's a focused bet on driving going electric, so it swings with EV demand and government incentives.
MFUT: A trend-following program trading futures on stocks, bonds, currencies and commodities worldwide, riding moves up or down wherever they appear. It's a diversifier meant to make money in extended market slides, and it can churn sideways, losing a little, when markets have no clear trend.
MMAX: Large US stocks with the strongest shield iShares offers in this series: over each year starting in March it aims to absorb as much of any loss as options allow, in exchange for a low cap on gains. It suits cautious investors who want stock exposure with minimal downside.
MNVT: A concentrated portfolio of roughly fifteen to thirty-five fast-growing companies from the US and abroad, heavy on technology and newer industries like crypto mining, electric vehicles and space. It's a high-conviction growth bet: big winners can carry it, and individual losers can hurt just as much.
NACP: Large and mid-sized US companies scored on how well they empower minority communities, from board diversity to supplier and lending practices, developed with the NAACP. It works like a broad core holding, technology-led, with the social score, rather than the industry mix, as the main difference from the market.
NSIV: Large US companies trading below what the manager thinks they are worth, spread across banks, technology, health care and industrials. It's an actively managed value holding for the core of a portfolio, and like most value funds it can trail when expensive growth stocks lead the market.
NULC: Large and mid-sized US companies that pass environmental, social and governance screens, so some heavy polluters and controversial industries are left out. Technology is over two-fifths, making it a tech-led core holding whose difference from the broad market is the ESG filter, not the industry mix.
OTAX: US companies of all sizes chosen by a model that favors profitable firms, managed with taxes in mind: gains are deferred and losses harvested where possible. It works as a core stock holding for taxable accounts, where the tax management, not the stock mix, is the main event.
PAYR: High-dividend large and mid-sized companies, spread evenly across banks, utilities, staples and energy, with an options overlay that sells some upside to add extra income. It's built to pay out more than a plain dividend fund, at the cost of trailing when markets run hard.
PBJL: Large US stocks with a buffer designed to absorb the first fifth of any loss over each year starting in July, in exchange for a cap on gains. The terms reset every July, so buying partway through the year changes how much buffer is actually left.
PRAY: Companies from the US and abroad that pass a biblically responsible screen, leaving out businesses tied to things like abortion, gambling and adult entertainment. It's a faith-based core stock holding, technology-led and global, where the values screen decides what can be owned at all.
REGS: Large US growth companies picked by an active manager, with technology at about half the fund and internet, consumer and health care names behind it. It plays the growth role beside a core holding, and its active picks mean it can drift well away from the broad market's mix.
RWEM: Emerging market companies chosen by a quantitative model with human oversight, leaning heavily toward Asian technology at over two-fifths of the fund. It's an actively run take on emerging markets: chip giants dominate, so it behaves more like a tech fund than the typical bank-heavy emerging markets mix.
SAGP: Small and mid-sized companies around the world chosen for an unusual signal: how actively they lobby the US government in Washington. The theory is that firms working to shape policy benefit from it; the mix leans toward health care and industrial companies and changes as lobbying patterns shift.
SASS: A concentrated portfolio of US companies the manager sees as undervalued, led by industrial firms at about a third, with technology and health care behind. High conviction is the style: a short list of best ideas means bigger swings than a broad fund when picks go wrong, or right.
SLJY: Small silver mining companies, with call options sold against the position to generate extra income, plus some direct exposure to silver itself. It turns a volatile corner of the market into an income play: the option premiums cushion drops a little but cap the big rallies miners are known for.
SMOM: US stock market sectors held through sector funds, weighted by momentum, so whichever industries have been rising most get the biggest share. Right now that means technology and energy lead; the rotating mix is the point, and it can whipsaw when sector leadership changes suddenly.
STXV: Large US companies trading at lower prices relative to their earnings and assets, led by banks at about a fifth, with health care and energy close behind. It's a value-style core holding from a manager known for skipping social screens, and value stocks can lag for long stretches when growth is in favor.
SURI: An opportunistic fund concentrated in biotech, drug and life science companies, with room for a few big side bets in other areas like energy pipelines. It's built around company milestones such as trial results and approvals, so it can jump or drop sharply on single pieces of news.
TMFE: One hundred US companies picked for using their money efficiently, drawn from stocks recommended by Motley Fool analysts. Technology is the biggest slice at a bit over a third; the Fool's research list is the starting point, which makes it a curated growth-leaning core rather than the whole market.
WDTE: An income strategy built on the largest US stocks, selling options frequently to turn market moves into cash distributions paid every week. The weekly payout is the draw; the options cap how much it can gain in rallies, so it trades upside for a steady stream of cash.
WLTG: A growth portfolio mixing individual stocks with other funds, tilted by a rules-based system that looks for positive trends and strong earnings. Technology is about a third; the tactical shifts between growth areas and safer spots are what set it apart from a static growth fund.
XC: Emerging market companies with three big exclusions: nothing from China, Taiwan or South Korea, and no state-owned companies. Banks are the biggest slice at about a third; the result is an emerging markets fund weighted toward India, the Middle East and Latin America instead of East Asia.
XUDV: Large US companies chosen by a formula that boosts dividend yield while trying to keep swings near the market's, led by banks, food and phone companies. It's a dividend-tilted core holding: the booster approach means a higher payout than the broad market, though not the highest yield available.
